name: Retainers
lead: Orthodontic retainers are appliances worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their corrected positions. Teeth can drift back toward their former positions (relapse) because of recoil of gum fibers, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued jaw growth.[1]

Common types are Hawley retainers (a wire and acrylic palate plate), vacuum-formed clear retainers, and fixed retainers bonded behind the teeth. How long they are worn is set by the treating orthodontist and may be indefinite.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are also discussed in connection with mewing and jaw or palate development, with some users asking whether wearing them could restrict maxillary growth. No studies cited here test that question.

paras: A Hawley retainer is a wire running across the front teeth anchored in an acrylic palate plate; it is adjustable and one of the oldest designs, named for Charles A. Hawley. Reported drawbacks include appearance, effect on speech, fracture risk and weaker control of the lower front teeth.[2] Acrylic (polymethyl methacrylate) is widely used in prosthodontics and in making orthodontic retainers.[3]

Vacuum-formed retainers are clear shells over the whole arch; they are less visible and cheaper and are usually worn overnight. Fixed retainers are wires bonded to the back of the front teeth, usually the six front teeth or just the canines, and need less patient cooperation but are harder to clean.[2] Begg, Barrer and app-linked retainers also exist.[2] Direct-bonded retainers were described in the clinical literature by the 1970s.[4]

Retainers rely on gum fibers adapting to the new tooth position, which is why relapse can occur if they are not worn as directed. Fixed retainers are described as performing best for holding the lower incisors, with vacuum-formed retainers better than other removable types.[2]

Vacuum-formed retainers worn while eating or after sugary drinks can trap sugars against the teeth, and can break in people who grind their teeth. Hawley retainers can affect speech, and poorly cleaned retainers of any type can lead to plaque, cavities and gum inflammation. Very hot water can warp removable retainers.[2]

Users on looksmax.org have started threads asking whether retainers stop or reduce palate growth in teenagers, whether wearing them undoes mewing progress, and what to do with retainers after treatment.[5][6][7] One poster who had clear aligners at about age 11 or 12 wrote that years in a retainer sized for a younger child may have left the upper jaw behind the lower, and described stopping the retainer and adding mewing and chewing.[5] Others discuss wearing retainers to keep teeth stable before planned jaw surgery.[8]

No studies found on retainers and facial or palatal growth. Clinical reports of retainers concern tooth stability and hygiene; early clinical experience with direct-bonded retainers was reported in 1977.[4]

timeline.event: Clinical experience with direct-bonded orthodontic retainers reported in the American Journal of Orthodontics.[4]

lore.intro: Retainer threads on looksmax.org mostly ask whether routine post-braces retainers conflict with mewing, jaw growth or planned expansion surgery.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Retainers worn through the teen years can stop the palate or maxilla from developing.
claims.believers: Posters describe cases where they wore retainers for several years after treatment and later felt the upper jaw looked recessed, attributing this to the retainer fixing the arch at its early size.[5][6]
claims.experts: Orthodontic references describe retainers as holding tooth position against relapse and do not describe an effect on palatal or maxillary growth.[2] No studies found testing this claim.

claims.claim: Wearing a retainer at night reverses the progress made by mewing during the day.
claims.believers: Forum users ask whether the retainer undoes daytime tongue posture, and some propose skipping retainer nights.[7]
claims.experts: Orthodontic sources describe retainers as maintaining tooth position; no published study has examined their interaction with tongue posture practices.[2]

claims.claim: Retainers are needed to hold teeth stable before or between jaw procedures.
claims.believers: A user planning bimaxillary surgery wrote that he would get night retainers so his teeth would not shift in the meantime.[8]
claims.experts: Retainers are described as preventing relapse after tooth movement, and fixed retainers are recommended where relapse is more likely.[2]

card.summary: Plastic or wire appliances that keep teeth where braces put them; forums debate whether they hold back jaw growth, which nobody has tested.
card.note: Claims that retainers stunt palate growth are untested; wearing instructions come from the treating orthodontist.

quick.overview:
Retainers are worn after braces or aligners to keep teeth from drifting back. Types include Hawley retainers, clear vacuum-formed trays and wires bonded behind the front teeth.

On looksmax.org, some users worry that retainers restrict palate growth or undo mewing. No studies cited here address that.
quick.mechanism: They hold teeth in position while the gum fibers and bone adapt to the new arrangement. Fixed bonded wires work continuously; removable ones depend on being worn.
quick.risks: Reported problems include decay when clear retainers are worn while eating or drinking sugary fluids, plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned, speech effects from Hawley designs, breakage and warping.
